utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we want to know whether the both parties have prepared lists for the documents. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, yes, we've prepared and submitted a list of exhibits for today's witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Oh, for today's? I mean for yesterday's.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we had submitted that last week, the list that had to do with the witness Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President I have prepared what I can only say is a draft. I -- it's right here in my hand but I wanted to proof it again frankly before the next break if the Chamber would allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Of course, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The problem is without the translation we could not admit all those documents into evidence at this stage so I hope both parties could submit their objections in written form concerning the other side's documents tendered. Mr. Krsnik, are you ready for your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, would you please bring the witness in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please take the solemn declaration, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Examined by Mr. Krsnik:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know that this may be the first situation in which you have been called as a witness to this Tribunal. Just relax. You'll get used to this atmosphere. I will now give you a few instructions since we are speaking the same language. You can check the terminal in front of you. When the dot appears at the end of the sentence, it's a sign that it's the end of a statement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the beginning, every witness is required to introduce himself. Could you tell us where and when you were born, what education you have, and where were you present in 1990, very briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, my name is Bozo Rajic, I was born on the 22nd of July in 1943 in Kupres, Bosnia-Herzegovina. I'm married, a father of two children, was never criminally punished and this is my first appearance in front of this Tribunal. In the place in which I was born, I graduated from the elementary school. I graduated in Bugojno from the economic, technical secondary school. I became a graduate mechanical engineer in the university of Stup. Before the war and after the war, I lived in Kupres. I carried out all sorts of jobs and functions in the public administration in financial, commercial affairs, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell me, until 1990, were you politically active?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: Until the year 1990, I was not politically active in any way. I was not a member of the then only political party, the League of Communists of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you not become politically active? Did you not accept the plan of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: There are many reasons. I'll try to focus on three. One, Marxism as an ideology, as a view of life was in contradiction with my understanding of the world relations between people and nations. The second reason, Marxism, Marxism entailed membership in the League of Communists, atheism -- very aggressive atheism was also entailed which is in full disharmony with my Catholic upbringing and the third reason, the Communist Party through its structure, its philosophy, and its internal freedoms was stifling all sorts of creativity and I could not perform my work without having the freedom of creative activity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you activated in 1990 in political terms and if you have become politically active at that time, within the framework of which party and perhaps you could tell us in a few words how and where you did it.

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: In 1990, the wave of democratic change also came to my father land, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I decided to be a politically-active person. First and foremost because I was convinced that every person with democratic beliefs, a person who can help in creating life, can not remain politically uncommitted and non-active. The reason to enter the party which I opted for, the Croatian Democratic Community, was founded in my political attitude towards the realities in which I was living, and my desire for the realities to be improved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us very briefly what functions, so as to inform the Chamber very briefly about it, what were the functions that you were performing in 1990 and onward?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: In -- at that time, I performed a variety of functions, some of them on a voluntary basis and others on a professional basis. In 1990, in September, I was appointed chairman of the municipal committee of the Croatian Democratic Community in Kupres. I was re-elected to the same post at the beginning of 1992. After the war, and upon the occupation of my town by the Serbian aggressor forces, I went to Montenegro first, to Grude and then to Mostar. My first professional job that I was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. My apologies to Mr. Krsnik and also to the witness, but a clarification. The English translation that we are getting for the name of the organisation is Croatian Democratic Community which is -- I want to make sure that I'm understanding whether we are talking about the political party, the HDZ as opposed to the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. It was my understanding or belief that the English translation HDZ is Croatian Democratic Union and if that's the party that we are talking about, I think it would be of assistance to all of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik, could you make some clarification for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, Witness, these translations are always a problem. Well maybe not always a problem because the interpreters have a difficult job to do. In fact, you spoke about a Croatian Democratic Union as a political party that you were in fact the President of the municipal committee of the HDZ. Could you please make it quite sure that distinction is made between HDZ and HZHB?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, I will. So the first professional job that I took over in the course of the war was assistant deputy commander of the defence forces. I'm talking about the HZ HB of the Croatian Defence counsel. At the end of 1992, I ceased performing this job and I was appointed Minister of Defence of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I continued to perform this function until the beginning of the summer in 1993, and then I was appointed director general of the Herceg Bosnian press agency where I performed my duty until the end of 1995. Then I was appointed Minister of Reconstruction and Development in the government of the Herceg-Bosna Republic of Herceg-Bosna and finally in January, 1996, I was appointed at the assembly of the party, president of the Croatian Democratic Community -- union, sorry, union, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I continued to perform this function until May, 1996, and when my term of office expired, I did not stand for re-election. I withdrew from political life. I remained a member of HDZ without any political functions either in the party or in the enforcement bodies of the HDZ. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Witness, I have to remind you that whatever you said has to be translated into the other two languages. So take your time and speak slowly. The interpreters had a difficult time to follow you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I am inexperienced in these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rajic, I have to ask you again, here in the transcript it says you were deputy commander of the HZ HB defence council. In fact, deputy chief of the defence council. Is in fact this a military or a civilian function? Could you describe for us this function?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: In Croatian, the word "prestonic herda" [phoen] is below minister. However, that department was responsible for defence-related matters. And I was assistant head of the defence department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry I have to interrupt you once again because the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. interpretation is wrong. Is it in Croatia or in Croatian language, the word?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: I said, council in the Croatian language.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes but we are sorry but what it says is in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: I believe I said all that is important regarding my activities between 1998 --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But was it a civilian or military duty; that was my last question when you were the assistant head?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: That was the defence department and I was one of the assistants because there were a number of assistants.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And will the counsel also please break after the witness's answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Be so kind, Witness. Tell us what prompted you to join politics or, rather, to become a member of the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: Of course, like everybody else, I had my political attitude towards the most fundamental things in life. In the programme of the Croat democratic union, I found three definitions which for me were of outstanding importance. One, HDZ offered the reconciliation of the Croat people, which, due to historical developments, notably in World War II, was ideologically on two opposed sides and I knew that without reconciliation, we stood no political chance and the HDZ was the only one which offered that. The second definition in the programme was a clear request to rearrange relations in the then state of Yugoslavia with a view to much larger and fuller political and economic autonomy, degree of autonomy of the republics without excluding the possibility of the establishment of an independent Croat state. And the third reason, the Croat democratic union was the only Croat party guaranteeing that it would fight equally actively for the rights of Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Rajic, and where did -- when did the establishment of the HDZ in the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina begin?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: Well, it varied from municipality to municipality. In my municipality, in Kupres, the party was established in early June, 1990. In other municipalities I wouldn't know the details but be that as it may, it was a time between April and September, 1990.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there this party, I mean the HDZ autonomous, did it act autonomously and in what areas?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: May I remind you that at that time, there was a joint state called Yugoslavia and that it was made of six republics and two autonomous provinces. The HDZ was organised so as to be able to operate across the state and it also did in the territory of two socialist republics, Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether other parties acted in the same manner, across Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. For instance, the party for democratic action, with its seat in Sarajevo, and was active in Croatia and in Slovenia and in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rajic, what were the principal definitions and programmatic tasks of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe it is imperative to make -- to make an explanation with regard to this answer. Namely, we who were carrying out the programme of the democratic union of Bosnia-Herzegovina pursued goals that were not very ambitious before the war. They were very modest, that is, as measured with what would then happen during the war. Those goals were the overthrow of the communist system, the establishment of a democratic, pluralistic society, the transformation of nobodies, the so-called socially-owned property into private property, promotion of democracy, market, protection of human rights and freedoms, integration in the western political and security system. I believe that these were realistic expectations and they were not made of a maniac. However, the war came and the war disrupted everything. And instead of peace time goals, we had to look for solutions for what the war had brought about and before it the imminent danger of war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rajic, I was about to come to that. And tell us how was the HDZ planning to regulate the relations? How was it planning to regulate the relations within Bosnia-Herzegovina in its political programme? I mean war and all the rest.

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: The Croat democratic union was well aware of the quality of the territory in which it acted. We knew that Bosnia-Herzegovina was a multi-ethnic community, that it has been one for centuries, but that there was very seldom any equality in it. And that is why we thought that it was imperative to organise Bosnia along democratic principles, starting from a triconstitution says the witness and starting from the fact that in Bosnia-Herzegovina the constitutional basis was made of three equal constituent peoples, Croats, Muslims, and Serbs. All our political thinking respected the fact that there were three peoples who needed to be ensured equal rights and equality of all citizens.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did the -- was the programme of the HDZ changed after the establishment, so when you say you pursued the regulation of relations in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and my question relates to that.

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: Our principles never changed. We remained faithful to the option that Bosnia-Herzegovina was the state of three peoples. But another question was imposed on us when attempts to reorganise Yugoslavia failed, how and where to place Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnic. As you know, we are not interested in the political issues. What we want to know is the relations between the three nationalities, the Croats, Muslims and Serbs, in the period of 1992 to 1993, in that area. And we are also curious to know how and in what manner the witness was appointed as the defence minister at that time and how the defence ministry was functioning at that period. We also want to hear something about what happened in Mostar area during that period. This is what we want to hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, by all means, Your Honours. However, -- well, I have to answer it. It is very difficult to understand the relations between these three peoples unless you hear what were the political platforms of these three peoples. It is difficult to understand things that followed unless we make the introduction. And I tried to make my questions as brief as possible so as to get the answer, that is, will be as brief as possible and I shall now move to the developments in Bosnia-Herzegovina later on but you will see by the -- by what the witness said that I've satisfied the criteria because with these witnesses not to waste too much time in order to be able to cover as many topics as possible, so I'm trying to do it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I'm just asking you to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: While we are on the history of the former Yugoslavia, you said something very interesting, Mr. Rajic. You said that Bosnia-Herzegovina had been multi-ethnic for centuries, but there was little equality. Now, before you go on to deal with the area of conflicts that we are concerned with, could you elucidate a little on that, that there was little equality? Who was on top and who was on the bottom, and why?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You heard the question of Her Honour. Will you answer it?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I shall be happy to answer to the best of my knowledge. For the past 500 years, Bosnia and Herzegovina has never lived as a free state, as its peoples and citizens would like it to. Its history unfortunately is the history of occupation, protectorates or dictatorships. As of 1463, when Bosnia was conquered by the Ottoman forces, that is the Turkish empire, until the arrival of Austro-Hungary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Sorry. I didn't mean you to go back that far. All I wanted you to deal with was the modern Yugoslavia, the modern former Yugoslavia, say since the end of the Second World War but not -- we know the history is very involved and fascinating but I just want to deal with in your life time. Thank you, and I'm sorry for interrupting you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I merely wanted to make this detour to remind you that for the past 500 years, Bosnia-Herzegovina was not -- has not been a free country. And as for the relations among its peoples, in the state in which I lived until 1990, from the formal point of view and legal point of view, they were equal, but all of us who lived in Yugoslavia or more specifically in Bosnia and Herzegovina, know that it was a state where the Serbs dominated and the state of the dictatorship of the communist oligarchy. For instance, the constitutional -- the constitution laid it out that every people and every individual had the right to use his own or its own language, but I know and it is common knowledge that thousands of Croats in Yugoslavia and in Bosnia and Herzegovina were brought to court because they had requested the equality for their mother tongue. The same held true of the representation in the most important bodies of state authority. The armed forces, the police, the foreign service, the customs, banks, large companies. They were all, by and large, controlled by Serbs. These are facts which I know, which I experienced in my life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's the first time anybody has actually told us that very simple fact. I didn't know until you started whether you were going to say the Muslims were in control or the Serbs. Thank you. Mr. Krsnik, it's your witness now, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, but you lead me. Yes, sometimes I do veer off the topic and you bring me back to the topic and thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us move faster forward, Mr. Rajic. Developments which ensued, can you describe briefly the events of 1990, of 1990, 1991; what were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the demands for the political solution of the dominant peoples and then we shall move on towards 1992.

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: Well, it is difficult to describe such a hard situation in a few words but I will do my best. Therefore, I said that other peoples, except the Serbs in Yugoslavia, wanted Yugoslavia to be organised as a confederation and that the republics be granted more political and economic room. The Serbs, lead by Serbia and Montenegro, and with the clear support of the former Yugoslav People's Army, refused any form of the establishment of equality of the republics and peoples. And when all the attempts to arrive at a democratic solution failed, first the Slovenes and then the Croats used their right to self-determination and voted for their independence and sovereignty, whereupon the greater Serbian politics responded with an open aggression, with a brutal aggression, which was preceded by a fictitious war in Slovenia and in 1991, Croatia was devastated, its cities burned, its population was expelled, and when the international institutions tried to help, decisions were taken which were good at first glance for the army to pull out from Slovenia and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which army, excuse me?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: The Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you have to say it every time, please?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: The Yugoslav army. However, it was bad and fateful that it pulled out or rather moved house to Bosnia and Herzegovina. In parallel with that, in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Serb Democratic Party performed autonomisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please explain what autonomisation means?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: This is a procedure which the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina used to proclaim Serb autonomous regions, in which their guiding principle was that where there are 5 per cent of Serbs or where there is a Serb temple, that is a church, then that is then -- that that then belongs to Serbs. The Yugoslav army armed them openly and to us, the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the Croat democratic union, were quite clear that aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina would ensue and that we had to do something to protect the Croat people biologically against disappearance, especially bearing in mind the fact that Slovenia and Croatia had become autonomous, had split away from Yugoslavia. So, counsel, this is the briefest possible explanation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us move on. What was the first act of aggression in Bosnia-Herzegovina and how were -- what was the attitude of other parties towards this act and how did other parties react towards the aggression against Croatia?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, at that time, there were three relevant political parties: The Serb Democratic Party, the party for democratic action and the Croat democratic union. Of them, each one of them brought together a number of [indiscernible] part of the representatives of its people. The attitude of the Serb Democratic Party to the aggression against Croatia was identical with the attitude of all other Serb parties in the -- in rump Yugoslavia and that part of the Serbian political leadership, which the Serb political leadership which organised the insurgence in the Republic of Croatia. The Croat democratic union of Bosnia-Herzegovina deeply sympathised with the sufferings of that part of the Croat people, which lived in the Republic of Croatia, and the Croats volunteers -- I mean them amongst the Croats, went to help in the defence of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean volunteers from the present Bosnia-Herzegovina, going to the present Republic of Croatia, is it?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have to bear this in mind. It is difficult to follow us who know all about the events we experienced, unlike those who did not experience them. So you have to be clear.

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, those who lived in Bosnia-Herzegovina, organised themselves in groups and went as volunteers to help the defence of the Republic of Croatia against Serbia's and Montenegro's aggression and the so-called Yugoslav People's Army. Unfortunately, I cannot gloss over the fact in silence that the party for democratic action, as the leading political force of the Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina, had pursued an inconsistent policy waivering and giving painful evidence with regard to the war in Croatia. When I say painful, then I mean that it was painful for us, the Croats, for whom Bosnia-Herzegovina is their homeland.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. What was this manifestation? How did it manifest itself?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: It is common knowledge that Mr. Izetbegovic, in his dual role, lacked the President of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the president of the party for democratic action stated that the war in Croatia, that is the aggression on Croatia is not our, meaning people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, not our war. This was followed by a statement in which Bosnia and Herzegovina -- in which the neutrality of Bosnia-Herzegovina was proclaimed in which he put it the Serbo-Croatian war, the war between Serbs and Croats, which is completely inaccurate and of questionable moral value, because it is common knowledge that that was not the war between the Serbs and the Croats but the aggression against Croats and their young state. And finally, the party for democratic action -- neither the party for democratic action nor the authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina did anything and nor did they react honourably, respond honourably, after the first act of aggression against Bosnia and Herzegovina, when the so-called JNA and the Serbia reservists attacked, destroyed and burned down the Croat village of Ravno in the southeast of Bosnia and Herzegovina and when the entire and exclusively Croat population was driven out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we now see tapes number 1 and number 2?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Lack of respect of ceasefire and new mobilisations on both sides, both here and Bosnia and Herzegovina and on the other side of the Sava and the Una are harbingers of more blood shed. Our duty, the duty of the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina would be to stop the bloodshed at all costs. However, as you could see, this was not in our power, nor could this be done by others who are more powerful so we cannot do this. What we can do is to refuse to participate in this madness. This is why, starting with the sovereignty of the republic, the views and stance of the Presidency and certainly interpreting the will of a vast majority of the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I hereby proclaim the neutrality of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Unfortunately today the time has come for us to need more courage to save peace than to participate in war. I would like to invite you to use this courage and to refuse to participate in this war. Beware of the fact this is not our war. We know what is our objective. This is not our army and they have to withdraw. Behind Listica, the row of passenger cars, trucks, et cetera, starts and continues all the way to Polog. We will stay here until they come back. The citizens have doubts as to the goodwill of the army, asking them why did you stop the tanks? They responded why so many tanks? Why here? The commander repeats yesterday's statement, we are moving towards the Bomisca Polje [phoen] Area. He thanks the republics and the municipal officials for trying to simmer down the situation. It turned out that the people at large do not want to enter a conflict, be brought into a conflict. Throughout the night, we had very good contacts and we went there without any incidents. It's difficult to estimate the number of the people who have gathered here, more and more people are coming in from the neighbouring villages, from here the army can only retreat and cannot proceed forward. It is for the third day that here in Polog, the army and the people are on the same positions. Nobody is willing to move. We've today heard that parachutists came to Vranica, around 1300 hours, Stjepan Kljujic, Jure Pelivan, Alija Izetbegovic and others came here to persuade the people to move and let the army through. You must have confidence in me because I was in prison for nine years as a young person for three years, and six years as an old man, I never wanted a pardon, and I cannot betray you. I can assure you of that. Thank you very much. Thank you very much. What I want to say is I may make a mistake, I'm trying to judge things as a human being and I believe that you should let the tanks through to allow the army to do their job.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this is where we can stop. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rajic, could you explain to the Chamber in what year, if you can recall, this statement was made by Mr. Alija Izetbegovic about neutrality, his statement, this is not our war? Well this is the first question. What was the year the statement was made? Did you see the programme yourself on TV?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I watched it on TV, in the news, and similar programmes, broadcast by the television companies of Sarajevo and Zagreb and I think that this statement was made towards the end of 1991, when the war broke out in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, in this second part, Listica was mentioned. What is the -- where is Listica, what is it? This second part of the tape showed us the tanks and Listica was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: Listica is another name used for Siroki Brijeg and this took place in the village of Polog on the road between Mostar and Siroki Brijeg, and it happened in May, 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever heard that Listica is a Muslim name for Siroki Brijeg? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: This is nonsense. Listica is the river that flows through Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting you. So you told us the year and the place where it was made. What was the problem with the JNA tanks and why did the people gather there to stop them?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: Can my terminal be put on once again, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you push button number 4?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The events of May, 1991, in the village of Polog where a row of tanks of the JNA were stopped by the Croatian people. Unannounced, with uncovered barrels and with live ammunition, the row was headed -- of tanks was heading towards a location and a destination that nobody was sure about. There were two versions. According to the first, they wanted to cross the Imotski and were aiming towards Split.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Imotski and Split were in which country?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: In the Republic of Croatia, towards the municipality of Kupres, i.e., towards the place of my birth. People did not let the tanks through without an explanation as to where they were heading and why.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Alija Izetbegovic convince the people who gathered there and was this the Croats who were there that he addressed and when these Alija, Alija exclamations were made, was this by the Croatian people?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: The municipality of Siroki Brijeg and its neighbouring municipalities are territories with almost 100 per cent Croat population. The people who gathered in front of the tanks were absolutely, exclusively the Croats, and they manifested decent, good respect of the President of the Presidency, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, and they manifested their respect for him and trust in him. However, they still refused to let the army through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the end, did the row of tanks get through after Mr. Izetbegovic's statement and to your knowledge, what happened with those tanks afterwards?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm familiar with that. People were convinced that they were heading for drill and exercise to take place in the Kupresko Polje field. They went on and stopped in the area around the Serbian villages of Gornji and Donji Malovan in the municipality of Kupres. And this is where they stayed until the beginning of the winter. Given the fact that I lived there, I know that due to their presence, every access to the forests there was blocked and that they fully armed the Serb population of Kupres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they attack Kupres, and what happened in Kupres?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: Not at that time. They did not attack it at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I understand.

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: However, the attack did take place on April 3, 1993, and after fierce resistance, which together with the Muslims of Kupres, we waged, the Serbian forces occupied Kupres on the night of April 6 to 7 in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the Serb population?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: The Serb population to the very last individual were expelled, their properties were looted. Their houses and properties burnt down. And what was not burned was later disassembled and taken away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, and again apologies to counsel and to the witness, I'm not certain whether we've got the record correctly. The English translation indicates that the attack took place on the 3rd of April, 1993, and then the next line down the Serbian forces occupied Kupres on the night of April 6 to 7, 1992. So could we just be precise in what year we are talking about, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the first and the second time, the witness said 1992. Perhaps the interpreters didn't hear it well enough.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me repeat the question, Witness. When was Kupres attacked for the sake of the transcription, please? Was that in 1992 or in 1993?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: Well, I hope that we understand the difference between the beginning of the war and/or the attack, and the occupation of the town by the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which year did this happen in?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the attack on the 3rd and the 4th and occupation on the 6th and the 7th?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Can you explain to us under what circumstances and how the HZ HB was established, when it was established for what reasons, is this a state, is it an association, what is HZ HB? Could you please explain this to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, while we are talking about the translation, it doesn't make sense what the witness has said in translation, that the town of Kupres was occupied after joint resistance and then all the Serb villagers were dismantled. It's the Serbs who -- let me see. The Serb population to the very last individual was expelled, their properties were looted, their houses and properties burnt down. Could that possibly be right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We said non-Serbian population, non-Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: That makes sense because it didn't translate that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Pinter has been requested to draw my attention to the transcript. I certainly am trying to focus upon the examination of the witness. But I am aware of the fact that we have to be very careful. I've noticed it the first time. I know that it's difficult for the interpreters sometimes to interpret another language. You know, even those of us who speak the same language sometimes are not paying enough attention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So can you please slow down? Can you focus, Witness, because this will also facilitate the work to our interpreters whose job is difficult? And they are performing it with a desire towards a mutual satisfaction. So we started with a question and how HZ HB was established, under what circumstances, how, and then to explain to the Chamber was this a state? Was this another community? What it was?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: Earlier ago, answering one of your questions, I spoke about the circumstances which led to the aggression against the Republic of Croatia. And the announcement of a certain attack against Bosnia-Herzegovina to ensue. While the Serb aggression was destroying Croatia, the Serb Democratic Party in Bosnia-Herzegovina performed a practical secession of about two-thirds of the state territory. It provided weapons to the Serbian population and sent out clear threats that through a war, Bosnia-Herzegovina will be affiliated with Yugoslavia. Furthermore, I emphasised that the legal government of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Presidency, through their indetermination and indecisive policy, were not a source of confidence either. They were playing around with the idea of a rump Yugoslavia, of an asymmetric model of regulations of relationships which certainly only gave to further concern and threat among the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, who, under no circumstances, wanted to stay in a Yugoslavia upon Slovenia's and Croatia's secession from Yugoslavia. We were aware of the severity of destructions in Croatia. Thousands and thousands of people were expelled, homeless people, and the final breakdown in the defences of Vukovar made it quite clear to us that we have to do something on our own. As a witness of those times in Bosnia-Herzegovina, I must say, very sincerely, that I did not believe in the ability of the legal authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina to be able to organise and efficiency resist an aggression.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rajic, I'll interrupt you here because I think this is the time of the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that I'm right. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We will resume at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Bring the witness in, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rajic, I have been requested once again by the interpreters to observe this break between the end of one statement and the beginning of another. I know that I'm the main culprit, much more than you. And we will focus. And whenever you mention a concept, would you please be kind enough to explain it to us? Distinguished Mr. Rajic, so we discussed the causes for the establishment of HZ HB. You told us in an introduction a few things about it. Tell me now, whether the reason for the establishment of the HZ HB was a search for the best model of self-organisation or was it something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I object to the leading form of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may put it another way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I'll put it another way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, generally speaking, what were the foundations for the establishment of the HZ HB, very briefly?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Earlier, I described the circumstances prevailing during the war in Croatia, and about the atmosphere that was present in Bosnia-Herzegovina. In the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina, we were fully aware that the aggression against a part of the Croatian people living in the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Republic of Croatia will not stop there, and that the Croats and the Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina will also soon be attacked by the same aggressor. The Serbs had already withdrawn from the main authorities and bodies of the legal authorities. The entire constitutional system of the defence, through the institutions of the so-called Territorial Defence, lost its reason to exist. Under these constitutional stipulations, we were supposed to defend the country, which will attack us, because it had already attacked the other republics. We were supposed to defend, on a joint basis, Bosnia-Herzegovina, all its peoples, and all its citizens, and yet we were a witness of an attack from within, preparations for an attack from within by the Serbs. The authorities were not providing any guarantees as to what would be the response to that, and this situation we gathered on the 18th of November, 1991, the legally elected representatives of the Croat people in the parliamentary bodies of Bosnia-Herzegovina, with a purpose of seeking the best manner possible of organising ourselves with the aim of defending the lives and the territories of the Croat people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This, Your Honours, has been the crux of our motives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, what could have been the alternative, had you not done this?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: The alternative was horrible, massive deaths of people, destructions, expulsions, possibly in a very black scenario even the disappearance of the Croat nation in -- from the territories of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but it seems to me that I still owe you an answer to an earlier -- to your earlier question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: Your question was whether the Croat community of Herceg-Bosna was a state, an association, or something of a different kind. I'm one of the participants of the very foundation and establishment of the HDZ and I'd like to assure you, Your Honours, that the only motive that we had in establishing it was the desire to establish a form which would prevent the genocide of the Croatian people to take place in this country. No other state was implied, although I know that there were subsequent attempts of reinterpretation along these lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rajic, in the transcript, once again, we have instead of HZ HB, HDZ. So I have to ask you, in connection with your answer earlier ago, are you one of the founders of HDZ or HZ HB?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: I'm the founder of both, but in my last answer, I emphasised that I am one of the founders of the Croat Community Herceg-Bosna, which happened on the 18th of November in 1991, at Grude.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rajic, at that time, what was the legal and statutory position of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: At that time, in those months, Bosnia-Herzegovina was still the socialist republic, as part of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it ask for independence? Did it get independence, so that we could define it as a sovereign entity?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: No. At that period, Croatia and Slovenia had already voted for their independence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting you. Were they also recognised as such by the international community?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: That is what I was going to say. It was announced that they would be recognised, these two states, but they had not been recognised as yet. While Bosnia-Herzegovina had not undertaken a single step or measure following the provisions of the constitution, to exercise its right to become an independent and autonomous state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, there is no dispute on those facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us now proceed to specific questions concerning HZ HB, and let me ask you what territory does HZ HB cover and to whom does its authority apply?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: The Croat community of Herceg-Bosna covers the territories of the municipalities of central and southern Bosnia, 30 of them, and six in northern Bosnia, which is usually referred to as the Posavina. But I wish to emphasise that we are referring to the territories of the municipalities and not the municipalities in their entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, again, Mr. President. I think it's very important that the record be precise in terms of the names of the various organisations, entities, et cetera. Now, on line ten of page 27, the translation is a reference to the Croat community of Herceg Bosnia and I think it should be Croat or Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna which is an important distinction in my view and certainly is one that ought to be made consistently in the record to distinguish between the HZ HB Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and some other territory of Bosnia or the Republic of Bosnia Herzegovina. It may be insignificant to some but for me and for the record I think is an important point that the English transcript always correctly identify these entities with precision and so I'm asking if we could clarify that, make sure again we are talking about the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, there should be some consistency in using of the terms. Maybe, Mr. Krsnik, you could make some clarification for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, Your Honours. But the transcript is always -- the transcript always follows the sentences said by the witness, but I will now try to clarify it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just heard the objection raised by our learned friends. Can you please clear the matter up?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. The Croat community Herceg-Bosna is not a party, but an organisational form which brought together Croats and their activities in a part of Bosnia and Herzegovina with a view to preparing the defence, and it always includes the inverse form of the name of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Because we first have the word Herceg and then Bosna in the second place. And I think that is how you can easily tell it apart from the Croat Democratic Union of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which is a political party on the turf of the entire Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did all the parties and people outside parties participate in the establishment of the HZ HB bodies in its organisation and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: The Croat community Herceg-Bosna, as I understand it, and the terms of its acts, is the -- an initiative of all the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina, a comprehensive initiative, an all round initiative of Croats, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, to organise themselves against -- in the face of the law make aggression and to sustain the vital functions of the people's life, until such time when an integral and stable state could begin to operate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, what was the attitude towards the Muslims in the HZ HB?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: Our attitude towards the Muslims, not only the Croat community Herceg-Bosna but also towards the Muslims in general, was sincere, friendly, and based on -- and cooperative. We knew that the aggressor had intended for us the same fates, the same fate, and that only if we were together, we stood a chance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what -- will you tell me if I put it to you, that in this courtroom, we had witnesses who belonged to the Muslim people and who said here that they had been discriminated against, fired from their jobs, from their schools, universities, from work. What would you say to that?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: In the name of the truth, one can -- there is only one possible answer, that is not true. There may have been some individual excesses but I do not know of any such examples from those pre-war days. What I can attest to before this Honourable Court is that with the Muslims in almost all the areas where we lived in mixed communities, we cooperated to the maximum possible extent in our preparations of the defence and that numerous Muslims worked at universities, schools, courts, and later on, including in the Main Staff of the Croat Defence Council, and there was a large number of them who fought in Croat units, that is in the Croat Defence Council. As for the jobs, one must realise that there was a war on, that the enemy was laying [indiscernible] everything and that includes economy, and that people went to defend their homes, their families, their people, that factories closed down, and that everybody lost their jobs regardless of their religious, ethnic or political affiliation and to make the truth complete, I must say that the situation was quite the reverse. In the areas where the Muslims constituted a majority, and it is quite natural that a larger share in all the offices is allotted to the majority people on both sides.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, now, the distinction between the HZ HB and the HDZ, as a political party. Are there any constant features in their political thinking, if you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, although life is dynamic and although everything is subject to change. And so is the politics subject to change, because of the changed conditions. So this also applied to the politics of the Croat Democratic Union and the practice of the Croat community Herceg-Bosna. There are, however, two constant features which remained unchanged ever since day one and to this day, and I believe that will also hold true of the future. First, we believed that peace was superseded every other interest and we tried to pursue that political ideal. Regrettably, we did not succeed in that, or at least not enough. And the second principle, which I personally respect very much, is that in Bosnia-Herzegovina, then, now, and in any future, the relations must be based on absolutely equal rights and identical solutions for all Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. three peoples. These, sir, are political constants.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the issue regarding staying in Yugoslavia or the rump Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is, I say, a derived question -- a derivative question and this situation which emerged, and that is why I pointed out the differences between the pre-war and war objectives of my party. We wanted Yugoslavia to be reorganised into a democratic state, community, with much looser ties as regards the central authority, but the Serbs refused it by offering the majority, as reflected in the principle "one citizen-one vote." We considered this unacceptable in a multi-ethnic state. When the Republic of Slovenia and the Republic of Croatia gained their independence, the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina and their vanguard, the party, that is, the Croat Democratic Union of Bosnia and Herzegovina, took a very firm position. Bosnia and Herzegovina should not and may not remain within the rump Yugoslavia under clear Serb predominance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Rajic. Thank you for these answers. Let us move on. Tell us what do you know about Tudjman, Izetbegovic agreement on the 20th of July, 1991? I will ask the usher. [In English] This is Exhibit P159. [Interpretation] Witness, I don't know if you've read it. Are you familiar with this agreement?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is it about? What is it about? What was it that was agreed upon?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: I'm aware of this agreement, of the 21st of July, sir, not the 20th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it was my mistake?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: Of 1991, I've known about it before. This is not the first time that I see it but now it has refreshed three details, and I believe it is important to point them out before this Honourable Court. First, measures of joint defence were agreed upon, and I deem it of utmost importance for the further development of events and relations. Secondly, the Croat Defence Council, as the armed force of the defence of the Croat people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, was recognised as a lawful formation, jointly with the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, serving the defence of the sovereignty and territorial integrity. And thirdly, under item 1 of this agreement, it is established that the two republics agree that in the -- that the future state order of the -- of Bosnia-Herzegovina will be governed by the principle of equal rights of the three constituent peoples, Muslims, Croats and Serbs, and the constitutional order will be founded on the constituent entities and which, when established, meaning constituent units, when establishing the constituent units, note will be taken, and I have to warn you of the order of words, ethnic, historical, cultural, economic, transportation and other elements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, who took part in the defence of the lands of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: These are two completely, fully lawful, fully legal, armed formations, bringing together, to an overwhelming degree, representatives of two peoples. The army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina made predominantly of representatives of the Muslim people, and the Croat Defence Council, likewise made predominantly of members of the Croat people of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Needless to say, along side them, the police forces are also fighting as linked with these two organisations -- with these two formations, and they also incorporate members of other peoples, ethnic minorities, and even Serbs. But also individual groups of volunteers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And which were these groups of volunteers, in the HVO, that is the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: I have already spoken how, at the time of the aggression against the Republic of Croatia, many Croats from Bosnia-Herzegovina and the diaspora the world over, went of their own will to assist the defence of the Republic of Croatia, and they joined the local army and police formations. When Bosnia-Herzegovina was attacked, many of them, a vast majority, who had left Bosnia and Herzegovina, went back to defend their homes, their families, their Croat people, and their homeland, Bosnia and Herzegovina. On the other hand, based on the principles of solidarity, compassion and sympathy with the Muslim people in Bosnia and Herzegovina and its army, the Muslim people and their army were helped by members of different peoples from different parts of the world, and in particular, from Islamic countries, and it is very important to emphasise that in the early stages of the war, that is the aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina, neither the Bosniaks, that is later on the Bosniaks, now the Muslims, nor the Croats had no difficulty with that. Quite the contrary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean that view changed subsequently?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, unfortunately. Yes, unfortunately. Those views changed radically later on and certain political representatives of the Muslim people in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the media connected to them endeavoured and some are doing it to this day, to -- in view of the fact that the HVO incorporated volunteers, some of whom had come from Croatia, they tried on the basis of that to build up an accusation of the Republic of Croatia's involvement in the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rajic, we have to speed up this and let us move to another topic and I want to ask you about the referendum, and my question to you is what was your attitude to the referendum and what was its outcome? Let us tell the Court something about those issues.

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: Counsel, sir, I apologise if I'm slowing down this trial. You and Their Honours may do something to speed it up. I have already said earlier, and may I remind you of this, that for the Croat people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, following the independence of Slovenia and Croatia, that to stay in Yugoslavia was absolutely unacceptable for them. In the steps of this option, the Croats of Bosnia and Herzegovina led by the Croat Democratic Union of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in an overwhelming majority of them participated in the referendum on the independence and sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and only for the sake of illustration, I need to say that the percentage of those who voted in the referendum, that is the percentage of Croats, as against the percentage of Muslims who voted in the referendum, was incomparably higher in favour of the former, of the Croats. And one other fact which is the material, the substantive truth. Alongside the well known view of the Serbs, without the votes of the Croat people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Bosnia and Herzegovina would be -- would not be able to achieve its sovereignty and independence in any way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us try to move on faster. Tell us, what preceded the war on a broader scale after the referendum? Perhaps we can also proceed to the topic of widespread war but limit ourselves to the Muslims and the Croats?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you will allow me, Your Honours, at least a small detour without which it is very difficult to answer this question. Now, as I see things, and on the basis of my experience, the war between Muslims and Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina was generated by the injustice towards these two peoples done by the Serb aggressors with inactive measures by the international community, on the one hand, and disagreements between the representatives of the two peoples concerned, concerning a model of an internal organisation and order in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Allow me to interrupt you. Tell me, in this Court, we often heard that this also had to do with the referendum, the so-called Livno issue, on the eve of all these events. The Livno issue concerning the question which the voters had to decide about at the referendum. Could you explain us this? Because other witnesses have testified to these circumstances and we are interested in your opinion. The Prosecutor tried to allege that the HDZ wanted a different question to be put at the referendum which would lead to a secession.

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: No, no. This claim is not correct, is not true, and for everybody to understand what this is all about, I shall repeat something. The Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in their entirety, almost 100 per cent of them, were in favour of the independence and autonomy of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which would have no political and/or legal ties whatsoever with the then-rump or any other future Yugoslavia. However, the fact that we were in favour of a sovereign, democratic and independent Bosnia and Herzegovina did not imply, and I know that it doesn't imply it even today, that the Croats of Bosnia and Herzegovina would accept any type of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We believed before the referendum that it was very important indeed for the sake of the future of that country, and for the sake of relations between Muslims and Croats, at the very referendum, to resolve the question of the future of the country and its internal structure and system. This is why we were not happy with the fact that the question put at the referendum adopted by the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina as such, and in favour of which voted also the representatives of the Croat people in their entirety, did not define and determine the internal contents of this common state. This is why, on the 9th of February, 1992, in Livno, a meeting was held of the central committee of the Croat Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina, during which it was decided that an attempt be made to change, to correct, the question to be put at the referendum so that it provide an answer, also to this question, as to what will be the internal structure and system of this state. This Livno question, it is usually referred to as such, was approximately as follows: Are you in favour of a sovereign and independent Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, a state community of three Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. sovereign and constituent peoples with equal rights, namely of Croats, Muslims and Serbs, organised within their ethnic territories, in brackets, cantons? Unfortunately, this additional definition of a state was not adopted under the need to save Bosnia and Herzegovina and to prevent its further existence within Yugoslavia, we appealed to the people to vote at the referendum. We voted in favour of its independence. We are conscious of major uncertainties that still had to be clarified. This is why, Your Honours, it is my belief, and I put it to you that this question was not, nor could it be, a question in the function of any disintegration of Bosnia and Herzegovina. On the contrary, it had to serve as additional binding force and substance of the new state. And later, the non-acceptance of fair discussions concerning this question by the representatives of Bosnian Muslims had become one of the causes of war, not the single one but one of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us go back to the question, what preceded a wide-spread war between Croats and Muslims so that we can continue along these lines? Very briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: Very briefly, given the differences and diversities described, certain local officials wanted to set up a system the way they understood it and saw it. And certain minor conflicts arose at the level of incidents. On three occasions, in Prozor, in Gornji Vakuf and in Travnik -- Novi Travnik, I am familiar with this because I was a participant in mixed Croat-Muslim delegations that went into the field towards the end of 1992 with the aim of stopping these conflicts and unblocking the roads and other transportation lines. Widespread war has a wider explanation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we then say something about the generators of those conflicts, as you see them?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: This entire gamut of possibilities is something that I will try to narrow down into two theses or, rather, statements. The first one is the following. When the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, within the aggression by the JNA, by Serbia and Montenegro, and with an active role played by already-separated Serbs within Bosnia-Herzegovina, expelled and ethnically cleansed people from large territories in eastern and parts of western Bosnia, a flood of hundreds of thousands of Muslims was pushed against, literally pushed against, a very small territory basically along the valleys of the rivers Bosna, Lasva, Vrbas and Neretva. Although a large number of these misfortunate people, as refugees, found their shelters in the Republic of Croatia and in a variety of west European countries, nonetheless, a vast majority of them were congested in this area, together with the local indigenous Muslims and Croats. Roughly speaking, about 70 per cent of the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time were living very closely together in slightly more than one-third of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. A new category, psychological new category developed, which I myself usually referred to as the density of life. The balance, in terms of ethnic structure that had existed, was significantly disrupted. People felt anxious and lost. I'm primarily referring to the Muslims but I'm also talking about Croats. Unfortunately the international community did not give a great deal of hope to anybody. It behaved in a pragmatic manner. It led us to believe that it either cannot or is not willing to stop the Serb military machine, and that it recognised the result of the war, the genocide and ethnic cleansing. Given this psychological atmosphere, people in this territory -- as this is my profound belief -- more out of desperation than for any other reason, started to fight for the remaining living space. This is the first fact that generated the war, and I'll very briefly now touch upon the second one. I spoke about it before. The lack of agreement between the representatives of Muslims and Croats concerning the system and structure, internal system and structure of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in due course became an ever-more prominent cause of war. Muslims insisted on a civic model of a state, which in a multi-ethnic community practically would imply the demand for a predominant position, not acceptable to a people with a smaller number of members, such as Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Croats, on the other hand, insisted that Bosnia and Herzegovina internally be regulated as a complex state mechanism whereby it was not important at all whether this complexity is the result of the fact that there were republics, cantons, provinces or something similar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Rajic. I didn't want to interrupt you with subquestions but then you answered them in advance and corroborated your statements before. We are now entering the year 1993 and the first question would be: What is the relationship between HZ HB towards the peace initiatives or all the measures and steps undertaken by the international community? What were the peace initiatives very briefly? Can you describe it to us, which will enable me to skip some of the shorter questions. It will, however, enlighten us, both the Chamber and everybody else.

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So I said it before, I have to repeat it time and again, because there is no other way to put these facts through. The Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina were the smallest people in terms of their numbers. Dispersed in a strategically adverse territory, of all the peoples, we could suffer the most due to a war, because our forces were the smallest in number. Therefore, our genuine option was a peace. Very often, to the detriment of justice, which eventually turned out to be the case. We accepted and embraced all peace offers and initiatives made by the international community's representatives, from Cutilheiro's Plan onward, to the Vance-Owen Plan, the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan, to the accords of Washington and Dayton, with very clear understanding, Your Honours, that I myself personally, just like a vast majority of Croats living in Bosnia-Herzegovina, were and remain to be fully aware of the fact that all these plans were and remain to be far from justice and equity, but we accepted them instead of war. Unfortunately, the representatives of the other two peoples did not follow or did not sufficiently follow the same logic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does -- did particularly the Cutilheiro Plan cause harm to the alliance of Serbs and Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, to your knowledge? Did the Muslims sign this agreement and, to your knowledge, what happened onward? What happened with this plan?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, there were many situations in which Croats and Muslims embraced the respective peace initiatives and offers. The Muslim political leadership subsequently, however, abandoned them. This was also the situation in connection with the Cutilheiro Plan. I'm convinced that the acceptance of the Cutilheiro Plan by these two peoples could have been an absolute guarantee for the fact that there would be no conflict between the two nations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which two peoples?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying that there would be no such conflict between them?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: It would be unfeasible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the move was made by?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Izetbegovic, the representative of the Muslim people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very briefly, the Vance-Owen Plan and the negotiations in Geneva, did anything specific happen in this context?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: I apologise for speeding up. Something similar happened. Both Croats and Muslims accepted the Vance-Owen Plan in Geneva as a solution which would organise Bosnia and Herzegovina in ten national provinces, of which, in terms of numbers, each people would get three but not the same territory-wise, apart from the tenth province, number seven, which is the Sarajevo province, for which a special status had been foreseen. Something which is perhaps remotely similar to a district. However, as I said before, unfortunately, Muslims once again abandoned a plan they had already adopted before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the first moment when they accepted the plan, what was the atmosphere among the Croats and did this have any reflection upon your personal fate? In other words, when did you become the Minister of Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina and whether this was a base, a foundation, for the Vance-Owen Plan and the negotiations in Geneva?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: It's a very complex question. However, I'll start at the end of your question. My arrival to the position of the Minister of Defence of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina is not linked to the Vance-Owen Plan. I came to this position before. In November, 1992, I was requested to accept this office, which frankly speaking, I didn't know either its scope or its possibilities. However, I assumed this position because down in my soul, I made an oath to the Croat people of Bosnia-Herzegovina and when there is a war, you cannot reject any position and duty, apart from something that every human being must reject, which is a crime. Sir, the explanation was the following. The Muslim side has seriously criticised the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina because of the fact that they had not assumed those posts of ministers and other official positions that the Croats were awarded to on the basis of the election results, because once the Serbs left us and decided to opt for their own side and waged an aggression, if the Croats too would fail to join the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the legitimacy of the government concerned would hardly be able to become sustainable. Understanding the gist of the problem, I accepted the nominations to this post, even though I did not know either where I would have my office, what I would do, what my powers would be, without an office, without a seal, without a salary, and without any material powers. In other words, I was fully aware of the fact that I'm entering or assuming a position which has a very high-ringing name but which however practically has no meaning. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I will now submit to you Exhibit D1/90. Before that, however, let me tell you that in this Court, we heard some witnesses who said that you gave an order which was an ultimatum to the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina or the Muslim people, and that perhaps because of this order, the war spread between these two peoples. How can you answer my question or my -- what I have just put to you?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: Sir, I am very grateful to you indeed for your putting this question to me in this Court. I have now entered a situation where I can speak about it, which nobody asked me to explain before. Your Honours, may I please be allowed to explain this document, which many people at home tried to abuse against me? It has to do with me, my person, my integrity, and my post.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, with your permission, earlier ago, you said that nobody invited you to do so before. Have you ever, over the last seven years, been in one way or another contacted by the representatives of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: No, by nobody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sorry for this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours we are now opening up a new chapter. We are approaching another break. I think I can finish the line of these questions within the next 40 minutes and since the time of the break is coming, I don't want to disrupt the schedule. I apologise, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, we will have our break and after that, we will hear your explanation on those documents. We will rise until 12.30.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I merely wish to apologise for this delay. I have some problems with the tapes and I simply had to make an additional check. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I have to remind you that we have to move faster.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have reached the last section of the examination. We are about to enter the final stage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rajic, we had -- I showed you your order. So will you please authenticate the document. Who signed it, the date and tell us all that you know about this document, alongside your explanation. And the document is D1/90.

utterances.speaker: BOZO RAJIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you please repeat your question to me? The question that you asked me before the break, because I'm afraid I haven't remembered -- I don't remember all the elements of that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, of course. My last question before the break was the following, Witness: That we heard witnesses in this courtroom who testified here that this order of yours was an ultimatum and as such that even -- and this is my arbitrary interpretation -- that perhaps this order conduced to broader-scale conflicts and I said: What do you have to say to that? What explanations can you offer? What occasioned this order? What kind of an order is it? And then to identify the document, that is give us the date there. Now, do you understand what I'm driving at now? So there are several questions because I see that you are giving us concise answers and I believe you will be able to answer it faster in this way?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, I read that document over the break and now I may be wrong about this but when we were referring to a document which was called the ultimatum last week, when -- sorry, when we had a witness giving evidence, I thought it was a document which was described as 216 which looks similar but the content and the tone are quite different. When we were talking about the ultimatum, I don't believe it was this document. It looks very similar but if you look -- sorry, if you look at the binder that we received originally from the Defence in the witness's binder, and then it ultimately wasn't used at Exhibit 216. I think you'll agree with me that the tone of that document is slightly different.
